Loss of fine touch in right upper limb.
Loss of pain & temperature in left lower limb.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe shape of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The spinal cord is cylindrical but flattened anteroposteriorly, extending from foramen magnum to the lower border of L1 vertebra. It has two enlargements (cervical at C5-T1 and lumbar at L2-S3) and shows longitudinal fissures (anterior median fissure and posterior median sulcus). It tapers inferiorly to form the conus medullaris. This shape is clinically important for lumbar puncture and understanding segmental anatomy.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord cylindrical shape, flattening, extensions, and conus medullaris
questions.modelAnswer: The spinal cord is cylindrical but flattened anteroposteriorly. It extends from foramen magnum to lower border of L1 vertebra. It has two enlargements: cervical (C5-T1) and lumbar (L2-S3). It shows longitudinal fissures (anterior median fissure and posterior median sulcus) and gradual tapering at its lower end (conus medullaris).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe the site of exit of spinal nerves from vertebral column.
questions.explanation: Spinal nerves exit through intervertebral foramina. Cervical nerves (C1-C7) exit ABOVE their corresponding vertebra. From T1-L1, nerves exit BELOW their corresponding vertebra. Below L1, the cauda equina (L2-S5 nerves) descends in the subarachnoid space before exiting through their respective sacral foramina. This somatotopic arrangement is essential for interpreting segmental neurological deficits.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal nerve exit above/below vertebrae and cauda equina arrangement
questions.modelAnswer: Spinal nerves exit through intervertebral foramina. Cervical nerves exit above their corresponding vertebra (C1-C7 exit above C1-C7). From T1-L1, nerves exit below their corresponding vertebra. The cauda equina (L2-S5) descends in the subarachnoid space before exiting through their respective foramina.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the site of termination of spinal cord meninges.
questions.explanation: The spinal cord meninges have distinct termination sites: the dura mater ends at the S2 vertebra (forming the dural sac terminus), the arachnoid mater also ends at S2, while the pia mater continues as the filum terminale (a fibrous band) that attaches to the dorsum of the coccyx. Below S2 is the lumbar cistern containing CSF but no spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: Meninges termination: Dura/Arachnoid at S2, Pia continues as filum terminale to coccyx
questions.modelAnswer: Spinal cord meninges terminate at: Dura mater ends at S2 vertebra; Arachnoid mater ends at S2 vertebra; Pia mater continues as filum terminale and ends at the dorsum of the coccyx (attached to periosteum of coccyx).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Give an idea about lumbar puncture.
questions.explanation: Lumbar puncture is performed to obtain CSF or inject medications. The safe site is between L3-L4 or L4-L5 vertebrae (just above or below the L4 spinous process). The patient is positioned on the side or sitting forward. The needle passes through: skin, superficial fascia, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura mater, and arachnoid mater to reach the subarachnoid space containing CSF.
questions.keyConcept: Lumbar puncture site (L3-L4/L4-L5), layers traversed, and subarachnoid CSF space
questions.modelAnswer: Lumbar puncture is performed to obtain CSF for diagnosis or inject medication/anesthesia. Site: between L3-L4 or L4-L5 vertebrae (just above or below L4 spine). The patient lies on side or sits forward. The needle passes through: skin, superficial fascia, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura mater, arachnoid mater to reach subarachnoid space (containing CSF).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate nuclei of posterior horn of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The posterior horn contains four main nuclei: Substantia gelatinosa (lamina II) carries pain and temperature; Nucleus proprius (laminae III, IV) carries touch and pressure; Nucleus dorsalis/Clarke's column (lamina VII) is the origin of spinocerebellar tracts; and the Visceral sensory nucleus receives visceral afferents. These nuclei are the second-order neurons in various sensory pathways.
questions.keyConcept: Four nuclei of posterior horn: substantia gelatinosa, nucleus proprius, nucleus dorsalis, visceral sensory nucleus
questions.modelAnswer: Nuclei of posterior horn: (1) Substantia gelatinosa (lamina II) - carries pain and temperature; (2) Nucleus proprius (laminae III, IV) - carries touch and pressure; (3) Nucleus dorsalis (Clarke's column, lamina VII) - origin of spinocerebellar tracts; (4) Visceral sensory nucleus - receives visceral afferents.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate nuclei of anterior horn of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The anterior horn contains motor nuclei organized somatotopically: Medial motor nuclei (medial column) supply muscles of neck and trunk; Lateral motor nuclei (lateral column) supply limb muscles, divided into anterior lateral (sternocleidomastoid, trapezius), posterior lateral (forearm flexors), and postural (limb extensors). The phrenic nucleus at C3,4,5 supplies the diaphragm. These are lower motor neuron cell bodies.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior horn motor nuclei: medial, lateral (with subdivisions), and phrenic nucleus
questions.modelAnswer: Nuclei of anterior horn: (1) Medial motor nuclei - in medial column, supply muscles of neck and trunk; (2) Lateral motor nuclei - in lateral column, supply limb muscles; (a) Anterior lateral (sternocleidomastoid, trapezius); (b) Posterior lateral (flexors of forearm); (c) Postural (extensors of limb); (3) Phrenic nucleus (C3,4,5) - supplies diaphragm.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe nuclei of lateral horn of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The lateral horn exists at two levels with different functions: T1-L2 contains the intermediolateral nucleus (cell column) for preganglionic sympathetic neurons (sympathetic outflow); S2-S4 contains the sacral parasympathetic nucleus for preganglionic parasympathetic neurons (rest and digest function). The lateral horn is absent at other levels.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral horn: sympathetic (T1-L2 via intermediolateral nucleus) and parasympathetic (S2-S4 via sacral parasympathetic nucleus)
questions.modelAnswer: Nuclei of lateral horn: (1) Lateral horn is present from C8-L2 (sympathetic outflow) and S2-S4 (parasympathetic outflow). (2) Sympathetic lateral horn nuclei: Intermediolateral nucleus (cell column of T1-L2) - preganglionic sympathetic neurons; (3) Parasympathetic lateral horn nuclei: Sacral parasympathetic nucleus (S2-S4) - preganglionic parasympathetic neurons.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe pathway of pain from face.
questions.explanation: Pain from the face uses the trigeminal pathway: 1st neuron (pseudounipolar) cell body in trigeminal ganglion → enters pons → descends to spinal nucleus of CN V → 2nd neuron decussates as internal arcuate fibers → ascends as trigeminal lemniscus → VPM of thalamus → 3rd neuron projects via posterior limb of internal capsule to postcentral gyrus (S1 cortex).
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal pain pathway: trigeminal ganglion → spinal nucleus CN V → VPM thalamus → postcentral gyrus
questions.modelAnswer: Pain pathway from face: (1st neuron) Trigeminal ganglion → (enters pons) → descends to spinal nucleus of CN V → (2nd neuron) decussates as internal arcuate fibers → ascends as trigeminal lemniscus → VPM of thalamus → (3rd neuron) via posterior limb of internal capsule → postcentral gyrus (S1 cortex).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate the neurons that form pathway of pain from body.
questions.explanation: Pain from the body uses a three-neuron pathway: 1st: Dorsal root ganglion cell (peripheral process receives pain, central process enters spinal cord via Lissauer's tract); 2nd: Substantia gelatinosa/lamina I in posterior horn (axon decussates in anterior white commissure, ascends 1-2 segments); 3rd: VPL nucleus of thalamus (projects to somatosensory cortex via internal capsule).
questions.keyConcept: Three-neuron pain pathway from body: DRG → posterior horn → VPL thalamus → cortex
questions.modelAnswer: Neurons in pain pathway from body: (1st) Dorsal root ganglion cell - peripheral process receives pain, central process enters spinal cord; (2nd) Neuron in posterior horn (substantia gelatinosa/lamina I) - axon decussates in anterior white commissure and ascends 1-2 segments; (3rd) Neuron in VPL nucleus of thalamus - axon projects to somatosensory cortex via internal capsule.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate the neurons that form pathway of crude touch from body.
questions.explanation: Crude touch from the body uses a three-neuron pathway: 1st: Dorsal root ganglion cell (peripheral process receives touch, central process enters and ascends/descends 1-2 segments in Lissauer's tract); 2nd: Nucleus proprius (laminae III, IV) in posterior horn (axon decussates and ascends in ventral spinothalamic tract); 3rd: VPL thalamus → postcentral gyrus. Crude touch crosses early and ascends contralaterally.
questions.keyConcept: Three-neuron crude touch pathway: DRG → nucleus proprius → VPL thalamus → cortex
questions.modelAnswer: Neurons in crude touch pathway from body: (1st) Dorsal root ganglion cell - peripheral process receives touch, central process enters spinal cord and ascends/descends 1-2 segments in Lissauer's tract; (2nd) Neuron in nucleus proprius of posterior horn (laminae III, IV) - axon decussates in anterior white commissure and ascends in ventral spinothalamic tract; (3rd) Neuron in VPL nucleus of thalamus - axon projects to postcentral gyrus via posterior limb of internal capsule.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate the neurons that form pathway of conscious proprioception & fine touch from body.
questions.explanation: Conscious proprioception and fine touch use dorsal column pathways: 1st: Dorsal root ganglion cell (peripheral receptor → central process ascends ipsilaterally in dorsal columns); Gracile tract carries lower body info, cuneate tract carries upper body info. 2nd: Gracile/cuneate nuclei of medulla → internal arcuate fibers decussate → medial lemniscus → VPL thalamus. 3rd: VPL → postcentral gyrus via posterior limb of internal capsule. These fibers remain ipsilateral until the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal column pathway: ipsilateral ascent in fasciculus gracilis/cuneatus → medial lemniscus after decussation
questions.modelAnswer: Neurons in conscious proprioception and fine touch pathway: (1st) Dorsal root ganglion cell - peripheral receptor receives stimulus, central process ascends ipsilaterally in dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis/cuneatus); (2nd) Neuron in gracile/cuneate nuclei of medulla - axon decussates as internal arcuate fibers and ascends as medial lemniscus to VPL of thalamus; (3rd) Neuron in VPL of thalamus - axon passes through posterior limb of internal capsule to postcentral gyrus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate the tracts that carry conscious & unconscious proprioception.
questions.explanation: Conscious proprioception is carried by: Gracile tract (lower body below T6) and Cuneate tract (upper body above T6). Unconscious proprioception is carried by: Posterior spinocerebellar tract (from Clarke's nucleus, lower body), Anterior spinocerebellar tract (lower body), and Cuneocerebellar tract (from accessory cuneate nucleus, upper body). The distinction is clinically important.
questions.keyConcept: Conscious: dorsal columns (gracile/cuneate). Unconscious: spinocerebellar tracts (posterior, anterior, cuneocerebellar)
questions.modelAnswer: Tracts for proprioception: (A) CONSCIOUS proprioception: Gracile tract (lower body) and Cuneate tract (upper body). (B) UNCONSCIOUS proprioception: (1) Posterior spinocerebellar tract (from Clarke's nucleus, lower body); (2) Anterior spinocerebellar tract (lower body); (3) Cuneocerebellar tract (from accessory cuneate nucleus, upper body).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe how unconscious proprioception is carried to cerebellum.
questions.explanation: Unconscious proprioception reaches the cerebellum via spinocerebellar tracts: From lower body: Muscle spindles/Golgi tendon organs → dorsal root ganglion (1st neuron) → Clarke's nucleus in posterior horn (2nd neuron) → posterior spinocerebellar tract → inferior cerebellar peduncle → cerebellum. From upper body: Same pathway but accessory cuneate nucleus → cuneocerebellar tract → inferior cerebellar peduncle. These tracts carry proprioceptive information for motor coordination without conscious awareness.
questions.keyConcept: Unconscious proprioception to cerebellum via spinocerebellar tracts through inferior cerebellar peduncle
questions.modelAnswer: Unconscious proprioception to cerebellum: (1) From lower body: Muscle spindles/Golgi tendon organs → dorsal root ganglion (1st) → Clarke's nucleus (2nd) → posterior spinocerebellar tract (or anterior) → inferior cerebellar peduncle → cerebellum. (2) From upper body: Same → accessory cuneate nucleus (2nd) → cuneocerebellar tract → inferior cerebellar peduncle → cerebellum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Give an account on pathway of pain from the face and body.
questions.explanation: Pain from face and body both reach the thalamus and cortex but use different pathways: BODY: DRG → Lissauer's tract → substantia gelatinosa → decussates → lateral spinothalamic tract → VPL thalamus → postcentral gyrus. FACE: Trigeminal ganglion → spinal nucleus CN V → decussates → trigeminal lemniscus → VPM thalamus → postcentral gyrus. Both pathways converge at thalamus and somatosensory cortex but use different nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Face pain uses trigeminal lemniscus (VPM); body pain uses spinothalamic tract (VPL)
questions.modelAnswer: Pain pathway from face and body: BODY: (1st) DRG → Lissauer's tract → posterior horn; (2nd) Substantia gelatinosa → decussates → lateral spinothalamic tract; (3rd) VPL thalamus → postcentral gyrus. FACE: (1st) Trigeminal ganglion → spinal nucleus CN V; (2nd) Decussates → trigeminal lemniscus; (3rd) VPM thalamus → postcentral gyrus. Both pathways converge at thalamus and cortex but use different nuclei.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Name the tract (s) carrying touch sensations of the face.
questions.explanation: Touch from the face is carried by two tracts: Discriminative (fine) touch uses the principal (main) sensory nucleus of CN V → ventral trigeminothalamic tract → VPM of thalamus → postcentral gyrus. Crude touch uses the spinal nucleus of CN V → ventral trigeminothalamic tract → VPM thalamus. Both pathways ultimately project to the VPM and postcentral gyrus.
questions.keyConcept: Face touch: principal sensory nucleus (fine touch) and spinal nucleus (crude touch) both via ventral trigeminothalamic tract to VPM
questions.modelAnswer: Touch sensations of the face are carried by: (1) Discriminative (fine) touch: Principal (main) sensory nucleus of CN V → ventral trigeminothalamic tract → VPM of thalamus → postcentral gyrus. (2) Crude touch: Spinal nucleus of CN V → ventral trigeminothalamic tract → VPM of thalamus. Both pathways use the trigeminal nerve and its sensory nuclei.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe lamination of pyramidal tract in cerebral cortex, internal capsule, brain stem & spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The pyramidal tract is somatotopically organized at each level: CEREBRAL CORTEX: Arises from areas 4, 6, and adjacent areas; descends through corona radiata. INTERNAL CAPSULE: Posterior limb (face most anterior, arm, leg most posterior). BRAIN STEM: Basis pedunculi of midbrain (medial 3/5), basis pontis (scattered bundles), medullary pyramids. MEDULLARY DECUSSATION: Arm fibers decussate first (become lateral CST), leg fibers lower. SPINAL CORD: Cervical fibers most medial, sacral most lateral.
questions.keyConcept: Pyramidal tract somatotopy: face anterior in internal capsule, arm medial in cord, leg lateral in cord
questions.modelAnswer: Pyramidal tract lamination: (A) CEREBRAL CORTEX: Arises from motor areas 4, 6, and adjacent areas; fibers descend through corona radiata. (B) INTERNAL CAPSULE: Passes through posterior limb (somatotopic: face most anterior, leg most posterior). (C) BRAIN STEM: Passes through basis pedunculi of midbrain (medial 3/5), basis pontis (scattered bundles), medullary pyramids. (D) MEDULLA: In pyramidal decussation, fibers destined for arm decussate first (become lateral CST), those for leg remain ipsilateral then decussate lower. (E) SPINAL CORD: Lateral CST has cervical fibers most medial, sacral most lateral.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe termination of pyramidal tract.
questions.explanation: The pyramidal tract terminates on anterior horn cells: The lateral corticospinal tract terminates on alpha motor neurons (final common pathway) and gamma motor neurons in the anterior horn of all spinal segments. The anterior corticospinal tract (uncrossed, small) terminates similarly but only in upper cervical segments. Corticobulbar fibers terminate on cranial nerve motor nuclei in the brainstem.
questions.keyConcept: Corticospinal tract terminates on anterior horn motor neurons; corticobulbar terminates on brainstem motor nuclei
questions.modelAnswer: Termination of pyramidal tract: The lateral corticospinal tract terminates on alpha motor neurons (final common pathway) and gamma motor neurons in the anterior horn of all spinal segments. The anterior corticospinal tract (uncrossed) terminates similarly but only in upper segments. Corticobulbar fibers terminate on cranial nerve motor nuclei in the brainstem.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe corticonuclear (corticobulbar) tract.
questions.explanation: The corticonuclear (corticobulbar) tract: ORIGIN from precentral/postcentral gyri and frontal eye fields; COURSE through posterior limb of internal capsule, basis pedunculi of midbrain, basis pontis, medullary pyramids; TERMINATION on motor nuclei of cranial nerves (III, IV, V, VI, VII, IX, X, XI, XII). Most CN nuclei receive BILATERAL input except the lower facial nucleus (mainly contralateral) and trochlear nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Corticobulbar tract: mostly bilateral cortical input to cranial nerve nuclei (except lower face)
questions.modelAnswer: Corticobulbar (corticomotor) tract: (ORIGIN) Precentral and postcentral gyri, frontal eye fields; (COURSE) Descends through posterior limb of internal capsule, basis pedunculi of midbrain, basis pontis, medullary pyramids; (TERMINATION) On motor nuclei of cranial nerves (CN III, IV, V, VI, VII, IX, X, XI, XII); (CONNECTIONS) Most CN nuclei receive BILATERAL input (except lower facial nucleus - mainly contralateral, and trochlear nucleus).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe tectospinal tract.
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract: ORIGIN from superior colliculus of midbrain; COURSE decussates immediately below its origin, descends in spinal cord (mostly upper cervical segments); FUNCTION mediates reflex turning of head and neck in response to visual and auditory stimuli (spino-visual and spino-auditory reflexes). It is part of the extrapyramidal system.
questions.keyConcept: Tectospinal tract: superior colliculus origin, immediate decussation, mediates head/neck reflexes to visual/auditory stimuli
questions.modelAnswer: Tectospinal tract: (ORIGIN) Superior colliculus of midbrain; (COURSE) Decussates immediately below its origin, descends in spinal cord (most fibers terminate in upper cervical segments); (FUNCTION) Reflex turning of head and neck in response to visual and auditory stimuli (spino-visual and spino-auditory reflexes); (CLINICAL) Lesion causes inability to turn head toward stimuli.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe rubrospinal tract.
questions.explanation: The rubrospinal tract: ORIGIN from red nucleus (magnocellular part) of midbrain; COURSE decussates immediately, descends through brain stem into lateral white column; FUNCTION facilitates flexor muscle tone and inhibits extensor tone; takes over function of corticospinal tract after lesion. Lesion causes decerebrate rigidity.
questions.keyConcept: Rubrospinal tract: red nucleus origin, facilitates flexor tone, takes over after corticospinal lesion
questions.modelAnswer: Rubrospinal tract: (ORIGIN) Red nucleus (magnocellular part) of midbrain; (COURSE) Decussates immediately, descends through brain stem, enters lateral white column of spinal cord; (FUNCTION) Facilitates flexor muscle tone, inhibits extensor tone; (RELATION) Takes over function of corticospinal tract after lesion; (CLINICAL) Lesion causes decerebrate rigidity.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Give an account on blood supply (cervical part) of the spinal cord.
questions.explanation: Blood supply of cervical spinal cord: Anterior spinal artery (from vertebral arteries) supplies anterior 2/3 of cord including anterior horn, lateral horn, anterior and lateral white columns. Posterior spinal arteries (from PICA or vertebral) supply posterior 1/3 including posterior horn and posterior columns. Radicular arteries from vertebral, ascending cervical, and deep cervical arteries reinforce the longitudinal arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical cord blood supply: anterior spinal artery (anterior 2/3) and posterior spinal arteries (posterior 1/3)
questions.modelAnswer: Blood supply of cervical spinal cord: (1) VERTEBRAL ARTERIES → anterior spinal artery (formed at medulla) and two posterior spinal arteries; (2) ANTERIOR SPINAL ARTERY supplies anterior 2/3 of cord (anterior horn, lateral horn, anterior and lateral white columns); (3) POSTERIOR SPINAL ARTERIES supply posterior 1/3 (posterior horn, posterior columns); (4) RADICULAR ARTERIES from vertebral, ascending cervical, and deep cervical arteries reinforce the longitudinal arteries.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the origin of anterior spinal artery & the parts supplied by it.
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery: ORIGIN formed by union of two anterior spinal branches of vertebral arteries at the medulla; COURSE descends in the anterior median fissure; PARTS SUPPLIED: anterior 2/3 of spinal cord, anterior horn (motor), lateral horn (sympathetic), anterior and lateral white columns, and gray commissure with crossing fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery: vertebral artery origin, supplies anterior 2/3 of cord including motor and sympathetic regions
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior spinal artery: (ORIGIN) Formed by union of two anterior spinal branches of vertebral arteries at the medulla; (COURSE) Descends in anterior median fissure; (PARTS SUPPLIED) (1) Anterior 2/3 of spinal cord; (2) Anterior horn (motor); (3) Lateral horn (sympathetic); (4) Anterior and lateral white columns; (5) Gray commissure (with crossing fibers).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the origin of posterior spinal artery & the parts supplied by it.
questions.explanation: The posterior spinal arteries: ORIGIN usually from posterior inferior cerebellar arteries (PICA) or vertebral arteries; COURSE descends as two vessels near dorsal roots; PARTS SUPPLIED: posterior 1/3 of spinal cord including posterior horn, posterior columns, and posterior white columns. Note: posterior spinal arteries are often discontinuous and depend on radicular artery reinforcement.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior spinal arteries: PICA/vertebral origin, supplies posterior 1/3 (sensory - dorsal columns)
questions.modelAnswer: Posterior spinal arteries: (ORIGIN) Usually from posterior inferior cerebellar arteries (PICA) or vertebral arteries; (COURSE) Descends as two vessels near dorsal roots; (PARTS SUPPLIED) (1) Posterior 1/3 of spinal cord; (2) Posterior horn; (3) Posterior columns; (4) Posterior white columns. Note: Posterior spinal arteries are often discontinuous and reinforced by radicular arteries.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate the arteries that give radicular arteries to spinal cord.
questions.explanation: Arteries giving radicular arteries to spinal cord include: vertebral arteries, ascending cervical arteries (branch of inferior thyroid artery), deep cervical arteries (branch of costocervical trunk), intercostal arteries (for thoracic segments), lumbar arteries (for lumbar segments), and lateral sacral arteries (for sacral segments). These reinforce the longitudinal spinal arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Radicular arteries: vertebral, ascending/deep cervical, intercostal, lumbar, and sacral arteries
questions.modelAnswer: Arteries giving radicular arteries: (1) VERTEBRAL ARTERIES; (2) ASCENDING CERVICAL ARTERIES (branch of inferior thyroid); (3) DEEP CERVICAL ARTERIES (branch of costocervical trunk); (4) INTERCOSTAL ARTERIES (for thoracic segments); (5) LUMBAR ARTERIES (for lumbar segments); (6) LATERAL SACRAL ARTERIES (for sacral segments).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Give an account on differences between upper & lower motor neuron lesions.
questions.explanation: UMN vs LMN lesion differences: UMN lesions cause spastic paralysis, hypertonia, hyperreflexia, clonus, positive Babinski sign, and no muscle atrophy (or minimal). LMN lesions cause flaccid paralysis, hypotonia, hyporeflexia/areflexia, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, and no Babinski sign. UMN affects descending corticospinal pathways; LMN affects the peripheral motor neurons or their cell bodies.
questions.keyConcept: UMN: spastic, hyperreflexia, Babinski positive, no atrophy. LMN: flaccid, areflexia, atrophy, fasciculations
questions.modelAnswer: UMN vs LMN lesion differences: (UMN) Spastic paralysis, hypertonia, hyperreflexia, clonus, positive Babinski, no muscle atrophy (or minimal); (LMN) Flaccid paralysis, hypotonia, hyporeflexia/areflexia, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, no Babinski. UMN lesion affects descending corticospinal pathways; LMN affects peripheral motor neurons or their cell bodies.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Give an account on two main tracts affected by hemisection of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: Two main tracts affected by hemisection of spinal cord: (1) LATERAL CORTICOSPINAL TRACT - ipsilateral UMN paralysis below lesion (controls voluntary movement); (2) SPINOTHALAMIC TRACTS - contralateral loss of pain and temperature (after decussation) below lesion. Posterior columns are also affected (ipsilateral loss of proprioception/fine touch).
questions.keyConcept: Hemisection affects: ipsilateral corticospinal (UMN paralysis) and contralateral spinothalamic (pain/temperature loss)
questions.modelAnswer: Two main tracts in hemisection: (1) LATERAL CORTICOSPINAL TRACT - controls voluntary movement; lesion causes ipsilateral UMN paralysis below level of lesion; (2) SPINOTHALAMIC TRACTS - carry pain and temperature; lesion causes contralateral loss of pain/temperature (after decussation) below lesion. Other tracts affected: posterior columns (ipsilateral loss of proprioception/fine touch).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe the effect of complete transection of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: Complete transection of spinal cord: IMMEDIATE (spinal shock): flaccid paralysis, loss of all sensations, absent reflexes below lesion. AFTER WEEKS: spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski. SENSORY: complete loss below lesion. AUTONOMIC: loss of bladder/bowel control, sexual dysfunction. All functions lost at and below the level of lesion.
questions.keyConcept: Complete transection: initial spinal shock (flaccid) → later spastic paralysis, total sensory and autonomic loss below lesion
questions.modelAnswer: Complete transection of spinal cord: (IMMEDIATE) Spinal shock - flaccid paralysis, loss of all sensations, absent reflexes below lesion; (AFTER WEEKS) Spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski; (SENSORY) Loss of pain, temperature, touch, proprioception below lesion; (AUTONOMIC) Loss of bladder/bowel control, sexual dysfunction; (LEVEL) All functions lost at and below the lesion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe the clinical picture of a patient with Brown Sequard syndrome.
questions.explanation: Brown-Sequard syndrome (hemisection of cord): IPSILATERAL to lesion: UMN paralysis below level, loss of conscious proprioception and fine touch (dorsal columns), LMN signs at exact segment level; CONTRALATERAL to lesion: loss of pain and temperature starting 1-2 segments below (spinothalamic fibers have already crossed). At lesion level: LMN signs at that specific level.
questions.keyConcept: Brown-Sequard: ipsilateral UMN paralysis + dorsal column loss; contralateral pain/temperature loss
questions.modelAnswer: Brown-Sequard syndrome (hemisection): (1) IPSILATERAL to lesion: UMN paralysis below; loss of conscious proprioception and fine touch (dorsal columns); (2) CONTRALATERAL to lesion: Loss of pain and temperature starting 1-2 segments below (spinothalamic); (3) At lesion level: LMN signs at exact segment, and loss of all sensations at that level.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe the effect of anterior spinal artery occlusion.
questions.explanation: Anterior spinal artery occlusion: AREA AFFECTED is the anterior 2/3 of spinal cord. CLINICAL features: bilateral loss of motor function (anterior horn involvement) → flaccid then spastic paralysis; bilateral loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic tracts); PRESERVED: dorsal column functions (proprioception, vibration, fine touch) bilaterally since posterior columns are spared.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery occlusion: anterior 2/3 cord affected, motor + pain/temperature lost, dorsal columns preserved
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior spinal artery occlusion: (AREA AFFECTED) Anterior 2/3 of spinal cord; (CLINICAL) Bilateral loss of motor function (anterior horn) → flaccid then spastic paralysis; bilateral loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic tracts); PRESERVED: dorsal column functions (proprioception, vibration, fine touch) bilaterally.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe sensory loss in case of syringomyelia.
questions.explanation: Syringomyelia causes dissociated sensory loss: (1) BILATERAL cape-like loss of pain and temperature (due to damage to crossing spinothalamic fibers in anterior white commissure where syrinx forms); (2) Touch sensation partially preserved (dorsal columns intact); (3) Proprioception preserved; (4) Loss begins in upper limbs and may extend. The key finding is dissociated sensory loss - loss of pain/temperature with preserved touch and proprioception.
questions.keyConcept: Syringomyelia: cavitation near central canal damages crossing spinothalamic fibers causing dissociated sensory loss
questions.modelAnswer: Sensory loss in syringomyelia: (1) BILATERAL cape-like loss of pain and temperature (due to damage to crossing spinothalamic fibers in anterior white commissure); (2) Touch sensation partially preserved (dorsal columns intact); (3) Proprioception preserved; (4) Sensory loss begins in upper limbs and may extend to trunk and lower limbs; (5) 'Dissociated sensory loss' - loss of pain/temperature with preserved touch.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A teenager girl discovered loss of sensation of her right hand and on examination, the doctor discovered loss of pain and temperature of distal part of the upper limb. Also, there was diminished pain and temperature on left hand. The condition was diagnosed as cavitations of the spinal cord.
questions.explanation: This case describes syringomyelia: a cavitation (syrinx) in the central part of the spinal cord. The patient has bilateral cape-like sensory loss. The pain and temperature fibers are involved because the crossing fibers in the anterior white commissure are closest to the central canal where the syrinx forms. Dorsal columns are spared. The most common site is cervical and upper thoracic segments where the central canal is widest.
questions.keyConcept: Syringomyelia: cavitation damages closest crossing pain/temperature fibers; spares dorsal columns

subQuestions.text: [TYPE: essay] What is your diagnosis?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Syringomyelia.

subQuestions.text: [TYPE: essay] Why the pain and temperature fibers are only involved in this case?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Because the closest fibers to the central canal & these cavitations are the crossing fibers carrying pain & temperature.

subQuestions.text: [TYPE: essay] Where is the most common site for such condition?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Cervical & upper thoracic segments of spinal cord.

questions.modelAnswer: (Diagnosis) Syringomyelia - a cavity (syrinx) in the central part of the spinal cord. (Pain/temperature fibers involved) Because crossing fibers carrying pain and temperature are closest to the central canal where the syrinx forms, they are damaged early; dorsal columns are spared. (Common site) Cervical and upper thoracic segments - the region where the central canal is largest.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 25 year old patient had an operation under spinal anesthesia. During recovery, he could not feel the back of his lower limb with difficulty in climbing the stairs by the right foot.
questions.explanation: This case describes normal anatomy during lumbar puncture: The correct lumbar puncture site is just above or below the L4 spinous process (L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace). The spinal cord normally ends at the lower border of L1 vertebra in adults. The meninges terminate at: Dura and arachnoid end at S2; Pia mater continues as filum terminale to the coccyx. These are safe landmarks because the cauda equina floats freely in the subarachnoid space below L1.
questions.keyConcept: Lumbar puncture site (L3-L4/L4-L5), cord ends at L1, meninges end at S2 (except pia)

subQuestions.text: [TYPE: essay] Where is the correct site for doing a lumbar puncture?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: just above or below L4 spine.

subQuestions.text: [TYPE: essay] Where does the spinal cord normally end in such a patient?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Lower border of L1.

subQuestions.text: [TYPE: essay] What is the level of termination of the spinal meninges?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Dura & arachnoid mater - end at S2, while Pia mater > ends at L1.

questions.modelAnswer: (Lumbar puncture site) Just above or below L4 spinous process (L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace) - safe area where cord has ended. (Spinal cord termination) Lower border of L1 vertebra (conus medullaris). (Meninges termination) Dura and arachnoid end at S2; pia mater continues as filum terminale and attaches to coccyx.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: An old man developed UMNL paralysis of muscles of lower part of the face while muscles of upper part of face were preserved.
questions.explanation: This case describes a UMN lesion of facial nerve: Upper facial muscles are preserved because the upper part of the facial nucleus receives corticonuclear fibers from BOTH cerebral hemispheres (bilateral representation). Lower facial muscles are affected because they receive mainly contralateral input. The parasympathetic nuclei are superior salivary nucleus (submandibular, sublingual glands), special lacrimatory nucleus (lacrimal gland), and nucleus of tractus solitarius. The terminal branches are temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular, and cervical.
questions.keyConcept: UMN facial palsy spares forehead (bilateral cortical input), affects lower face; CN VII has 5 terminal branches

subQuestions.text: [TYPE: essay] Explain why the muscles of upper part are preserved?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Because the upper part of the facial nucleus that controls the muscles of the upper 3 of the face receives fibers from the corticonuclear tract of both sides (bilaterally represented).

subQuestions.text: [TYPE: essay] List the parasympathetic nuclei of the facial nerve?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Superior salivary nucleus + special lacrimatory nucleus + uncertain nucleus.

subQuestions.text: [TYPE: essay] Enumerate the terminal branches of the facial nerve
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular & cervical.

questions.modelAnswer: (Upper face preservation) Upper facial muscles receive corticonuclear fibers from BOTH cerebral hemispheres (bilateral representation), so unilateral lesion spares upper face; lower face only contralateral representation. (Parasympathetic nuclei) Superior salivary nucleus, lacrimal nucleus, and the nucleus of the tractus solitarius (for taste). (Terminal branches) Temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular, and cervical branches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lesion of which cerebral area in left hemisphere causes motor aphasia?
questions.explanation: Motor aphasia (Broca's aphasia) results from lesion of Broca's area in the inferior frontal gyrus, which is responsible for speech production. In the dominant hemisphere, this is typically the left side.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area in inferior frontal gyrus causes motor aphasia

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Persistent pain in big toe is received in:
questions.explanation: The big toe is represented in the most medial and inferior part of the postcentral gyrus, which continues onto the paracentral lobule. The representation follows a somatotopic pattern with the foot at the medial surface.
questions.keyConcept: Big toe represented at medial postcentral gyrus/paracentral lobule
options: Lower part of post central gyrus.
Upper part of post central gyrus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Motor aphasia is due to lesion of the following area:
questions.explanation: Broca's area is located in the inferior frontal gyrus and is responsible for motor (expressive) speech. Lesions cause non-fluent aphasia with intact comprehension.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area - motor/expressive speech area

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Changes in personality and judgment occur in lesion of:
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex (anterior to the precentral gyrus) is responsible for personality, judgment, executive function, and social behavior. Lesions cause changes in personality and impaired judgment.
questions.keyConcept: Prefrontal area controls personality and judgment

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Injury to the left paracentral lobule leads to paralysis of:
questions.explanation: The paracentral lobule is the continuation of the primary motor and sensory areas onto the medial surface of the hemisphere. The left paracentral lobule controls the right lower limb (leg and foot) via the corticospinal tract.
questions.keyConcept: Left paracentral lobule controls right leg

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Injury to the right paracentral lobule leads to paralysis of:
questions.explanation: The right paracentral lobule controls the left leg. Since motor pathways cross (decussate), injury to the right paracentral lobule causes paralysis of the contralateral (left) lower limb.
questions.keyConcept: Right paracentral lobule controls left leg

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Reappearance of the grasp reflex occurs in lesion of:
questions.explanation: Area 6 (premotor area) lies anterior to the primary motor cortex. Lesions here cause reappearance of primitive reflexes like the grasp reflex, as this area normally has an inhibitory influence on these reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: Area 6 lesion causes return of grasp reflex

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Changes in judgment & intelligence occur in lesion of:
questions.explanation: The frontal lobe, particularly the prefrontal cortex, is responsible for higher cognitive functions including judgment, reasoning, planning, and personality expression. These functions are lost in frontal lobe lesions.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal lobe controls judgment and intelligence

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A lesion in the Broca’s area of the cerebral hemisphere leads to:
questions.explanation: Broca's area is located in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere. It coordinates the motor aspects of speech production. Lesions here cause motor aphasia with hesitant, non-fluent speech but preserved comprehension.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area lesion causes motor aphasia

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Match cortical area in left column with its lesion in right column: Prefrontal area.
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex is responsible for personality, social behavior, and executive functions. Lesions here commonly result in personality changes, including disinhibition and apathy.
questions.keyConcept: Prefrontal area lesion causes personality changes

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Match cortical area in left column with its lesion in right column: Broca’s area.
questions.explanation: Broca's area in the inferior frontal gyrus controls motor speech production. Lesions in the dominant hemisphere cause motor aphasia (difficulty producing speech with preserved comprehension).
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area causes motor aphasia when lesioned

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Match cortical area in left column with its lesion in right column: Area 6.
questions.explanation: Area 6 (premotor area) lies anterior to the primary motor cortex. Damage can cause release of primitive reflexes like the grasp reflex, as this area normally suppresses such reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: Area 6 controls grasp reflex suppression

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Match cortical area in left column with its lesion in right column: Frontal eye field.
questions.explanation: The frontal eye field (area 8) controls voluntary conjugate eye movements. Lesions cause inability to look toward the opposite side (loss of conjugate eye deviation).
questions.keyConcept: Frontal eye field controls voluntary eye movement

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Match cortical area in left column with its lesion in right column: Superior parietal lobule.
questions.explanation: The superior parietal lobule is involved in spatial awareness and stereognosis (ability to recognize objects by touch). Lesions cause astereognosis (inability to recognize objects by touch) and hemispatial neglect.
questions.keyConcept: Superior parietal lobule mediates stereognosis

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Frontal lobe in dominant hemisphere contains the following areas Except:
questions.explanation: Wernicke's speech area is located in the posterior superior temporal gyrus, not in the frontal lobe. The frontal lobe contains areas 4, 6, 8, and supplementary motor area.
questions.keyConcept: Wernicke's area is in temporal lobe, not frontal

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A lesion of frontal cortex in the dominant hemisphere results in all but one of the following:
questions.explanation: Receptive aphasia (Wernicke's aphasia) is caused by lesions of Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe, not the frontal lobe. Frontal lobe lesions cause expressive aphasia, contralateral paralysis, and behavioral changes.
questions.keyConcept: Receptive aphasia is temporal, not frontal lobe lesion

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Broca’s area:
questions.explanation: Broca's area is the motor speech center present in the dominant hemisphere (usually left). It is located in the inferior frontal gyrus and coordinates speech production, not sensory aspects.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area present in dominant hemisphere only
options: It is located in middle frontal gyrus.
It is present in the dominant hemisphere.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding motor speech center, all statements are true Except:
questions.explanation: Receptive aphasia is caused by Wernicke's area lesion, not Broca's area. Broca's area is the motor speech center; its lesion causes expressive/motor aphasia, not receptive aphasia.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's lesion causes motor, not receptive aphasia
options: Found in the inferior frontal gyrus.
Its lesion leads to receptive aphasia.
Lies in area of rami of lateral sulcus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Parietal lobe in the dominant hemisphere is concerned with the following Except:
questions.explanation: Facial recognition is processed in the inferior temporal lobe (fusiform gyrus), not the parietal lobe. The parietal lobe is concerned with stereognosis, proprioception, and spatial processing.
questions.keyConcept: Facial recognition in temporal, not parietal lobe
options: Comprehension of received auditory & visual information.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Astereognosis & receptive aphasia characterize lesions in:
questions.explanation: Astereognosis (inability to recognize objects by touch) and receptive aphasia (inability to understand language) are both features of dominant parietal lobe lesions, particularly involving the angular gyrus and supramarginal gyrus.
questions.keyConcept: Dominant parietal lobe lesions cause astereognosis

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Cortical areas in temporal lobe include all the following Except:
questions.explanation: Area for control of involuntary conjugate lateral eye movements is the occipital eye field (area 18), not the temporal lobe. The temporal lobe contains auditory areas and parts of Wernicke's area and facial recognition area.
questions.keyConcept: Involuntary eye movement control is occipital, not temporal
options: Area for control of involuntary conjugate lateral movements of eye.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The facial recognition areas are found in the undersurface of:
questions.explanation: The facial recognition areas (fusiform face area) are located on the undersurface of both temporal and occipital lobes. These areas specifically recognize familiar faces.
questions.keyConcept: Facial recognition in temporal and occipital undersurface

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The frontal lobe of the non-dominant hemisphere is concerned with which of the following functions:
questions.explanation: The non-dominant hemisphere (usually right) is primarily responsible for control of behavior, emotional expression, and visuospatial functions. The dominant hemisphere handles speech and language.
questions.keyConcept: Non-dominant frontal lobe controls behavior/emotions

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with inability to understand words and speaks non understandable words. Lesion is most likely in Brodmann areas number:
questions.explanation: Brodmann areas 39 and 40 (angular gyrus and supramarginal gyrus) in the dominant parietal-temporal region are responsible for language comprehension. Lesions cause Wernicke's receptive aphasia where speech is fluent but meaningless.
questions.keyConcept: Areas 39-40 lesion causes receptive aphasia

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A lawyer suffered a bad fall that resulted in head trauma. His motor, sensory, and language skills were intact after the incident, and he had no visual problems. In the following weeks, he began to lose interest in his work and did not seem to care much about his family. The trauma most likely affected the:
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex controls personality, social behavior, and executive functions. A lawyer losing interest in work and not caring about family indicates damage to the prefrontal area, consistent with frontal lobe trauma.
questions.keyConcept: Prefrontal lesion causes personality/behavior changes

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following fibers carry proprioception from the upper limb to the cerebellum?
questions.explanation: The cuneocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioception from the upper limb to the cerebellum. It originates from the accessory cuneate nucleus (lateral cuneate nucleus) and enters through the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneocerebellar tract carries upper limb proprioception

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Afferent fibers in the superior cerebellar peduncle include:
questions.explanation: The anterior (ventral) spinocerebellar tract carries proprioceptive information from the lower body to the cerebellum via the superior cerebellar peduncle. It decussates twice (once at the level of entry and once before entering the cerebellum).
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinocerebellar enters via superior cerebellar peduncle

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The inferior cerebellar peduncle contains:
questions.explanation: The posterior (dorsal) spinocerebellar tract carries proprioceptive information from the lower body to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle. It does not decussate.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior spinocerebellar tract via inferior cerebellar peduncle

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Superior cerebellar peduncle contains which of the following tracts?
questions.explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle contains the ventral (anterior) spinocerebellar tract which carries proprioceptive feedback from the lower limbs to the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Superior cerebellar peduncle contains ventral spinocerebellar

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The most lateral nucleus in the interior of the cerebellum is:
questions.explanation: The dentate nucleus is the largest and most lateral cerebellar nucleus. It receives input from the cerebellar cortex (particularly the lateral parts) and projects via the superior cerebellar peduncle to the thalamus and red nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Dentate nucleus is most lateral, projects via SCP

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The nucleus that projects neocerebellar efferent is the:
questions.explanation: The dentate nucleus is the main output nucleus of the neocerebellum (lateral hemispheres). It projects inhibitory fibers via the superior cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral thalamus (VPL/VPM) and red nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Dentate nucleus projects neocerebellar efferent

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The neocerebellum is anatomically located in the following part of the cerebellum:
questions.explanation: The neocerebellum (lateral parts of posterior lobe) is anatomically located in the posterior lobe of the cerebellum. It is concerned with planning and executing voluntary movements, particularly those requiring skilled precision.
questions.keyConcept: Neocerebellum in posterior lobe

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Hind brain (Rhombencephalon) includes all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The hindbrain (rhombencephalon) includes the medulla oblongata, pons, and cerebellum. The crus cerebri is part of the midbrain (not hindbrain), containing corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Crus cerebri is midbrain, not hindbrain

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nerve attached to the lower border of pons above pyramid is:
questions.explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) is attached to the lower border of the pons, in the groove between the pons and pyramid of the medulla. It is the most medial of the cranial nerves at the pontomedullary junction.
questions.keyConcept: Abducent nerve at lower pons above pyramid

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following cranial nerves is attached to the back of the brain stem?
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is unique as the only cranial nerve to attach to the posterior (dorsal) surface of the brain stem. It emerges from the posterior aspect of the midbrain, just below the inferior colliculus.
questions.keyConcept: Trochlear nerve is only CN from posterior brainstem

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: One of the following is not a content of the interpeduncular fossa:
questions.explanation: The interpeduncular fossa is a space between the cerebral peduncles. Its contents include the oculomotor nerve, mammillary bodies, tuber cinereum, posterior perforated substance, and cerebral peduncles. The anterior perforated substance is lateral to the optic tract, not in the interpeduncular fossa.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior perforated substance not in interpeduncular fossa

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A nerve attached to the cerebello-pontine angle:
questions.explanation: The vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) is attached at the cerebellopontine angle, along with the facial nerve. This is the angle between the pons, cerebellum, and olive where these nerves emerge.
questions.keyConcept: CN VIII at cerebellopontine angle

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a recess of the fourth ventricle?
questions.explanation: The lateral recess is the only true recess of the fourth ventricle. It extends laterally beneath the superior cerebellar peduncle and opens at the foramen of Luschka into the subarachnoid space.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral recess is a recess of fourth ventricle

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Medial eminence in floor of fourth ventricle overlies the nucleus of:
questions.explanation: The medial eminence overlies the abducent nucleus in the floor of the fourth ventricle. The facial colliculus (a elevation) is formed by the abducent nucleus and the facial nerve fibers looping around it.
questions.keyConcept: Medial eminence overlies abducent nucleus

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The superior angle of the fourth ventricle leads to:
questions.explanation: The superior angle of the fourth ventricle is continuous with the cerebral aqueduct (aqueduct of Sylvius), which connects the third and fourth ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Superior 4th ventricle angle leads to cerebral aqueduct

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A pontine cranial nerve that is not attached to lower border of pons:
questions.explanation: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) is attached to the lateral surface of the pons, at the junction of the pons and middle cerebellar peduncle. The abducent nerve attaches at the lower border, and facial/vestibulocochlear at the cerebellopontine angle.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal attaches at pons-middle cerebellar peduncle junction

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Brain stem includes all the following Except:
questions.explanation: The brain stem consists of midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata. The cerebellum lies posterior to the brain stem and is not considered part of it, though it is connected by three peduncles.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellum not part of brain stem

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Rootlets of hypoglossal nerve lie:
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve rootlets emerge from the anterolateral sulcus of the medulla, which lies between the pyramid and olive. This is the anterior surface of the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: CN XII between pyramid and olive
options: Between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Between lower border of pons & pyramid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Rootlets of glossopharyngeal nerve lie:
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve rootlets emerge from the posterolateral sulcus of the medulla, which lies between the olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: CN IX between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle
options: Between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Between lower border of pons and medulla.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following nerves lies close to the median plane in the transverse furrow between pons and medulla?
questions.explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) emerges at the pontomedullary junction, close to the median plane (between the pons and pyramid). It is the most medial of the cranial nerves at this junction.
questions.keyConcept: Abducent nerve most medial at pontomedullary junction

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures lies between limbs of inferior fovea?
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus is a bump in the floor of the fourth ventricle formed by the abducent nucleus and the fibers of the facial nerve wrapping around it. It lies between the limbs of the inferior fovea.
questions.keyConcept: Facial colliculus between limbs of inferior fovea

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Facial colliculus overlies:
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus overlies the abducent nucleus and the facial nerve fibers that loop around it (the facial nerve genu). This creates a prominence in the floor of the fourth ventricle.
questions.keyConcept: Facial colliculus overlies abducent nucleus

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The facial colliculus is formed by:
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus is formed by the abducent nucleus and the fibers of the facial nerve (motor root) that curve around it internally. These fibers form the facial nerve genu in the brainstem.
questions.keyConcept: Facial colliculus formed by CN VI nucleus and CN VII fibers
options: Abducent nucleus and facial nerve fibers.
Facial motor nucleus and abducent nerve fibers.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Posterolateral boundary of the interpeduncular fossa is formed by:
questions.explanation: The posterolateral boundary of the interpeduncular fossa is formed by the cerebral peduncles. These are two large bundles of descending fibers on either side of the midbrain.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral peduncles form posterolateral boundary

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The anterolateral boundary of interpeduncular fossa is formed by:
questions.explanation: The crus cerebri (basis pedunculi) forms the anterolateral boundary of the interpeduncular fossa. It contains the corticospinal, corticobulbar, and corticopontine fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Crus cerebri forms anterolateral boundary of interpeduncular fossa

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The cranial nerve that has the most medial attachment to the pons:
questions.explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) has the most medial attachment to the pons, emerging in the median line at the pontomedullary junction. The facial and vestibulocochlear nerves attach more laterally.
questions.keyConcept: Abducent nerve most medial pontine attachment

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards cranial nerve attachment to brain stem, choose the CORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: The vestibulocochlear nerve attaches at the cerebellopontine angle, which is the angle between the pons, cerebellum, and medulla. This is the correct matching for the anatomical location.
questions.keyConcept: CN VIII at cerebellopontine angle
options: Hypoglossal nerve - posterolateral sulcus of medulla.
Vagus nerve - groove between pyramid & olive.
Facial nerve - lower border of pons above pyramid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards the attachment of the cranial nerves to the brain stem, choose the INCORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve attaches in the sulcus between the olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle. This is a posterior attachment, not between pyramid and olive. The statement is incorrect about the groove location.
questions.keyConcept: CN XII between olive and ICP
options: Hypoglossal nerve - sulcus between olive & ICP.
Trigeminal nerve - Junction of MCP & basis pontis.
Oculomotor nerve - medial side of crus cerebri.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards medulla oblongata, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve (CN X) lies MEDIAL to the inferior cerebellar peduncle. Rootlets emerge between the olive and the inferior cerebellar peduncle. The statement in option D incorrectly places it lateral to ICP.
questions.keyConcept: Vagus nerve medial to inferior cerebellar peduncle
options: Olive lies just lateral to anterior median fissure.
Inferior cerebellar peduncle lies lateral to olive.
XII cranial nerve exits from medulla lateral to pyramid.
X cranial nerve lies medial to inferior cerebellar peduncle.
XI cranial nerve is attached to posterolateral sulcus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards pons, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: Cerebellopontine angle tumors typically arise from the vestibulocochlear nerve (acoustic neuroma/schwannoma) and cause hearing loss, vertigo, and later facial nerve involvement. Pontine gliomas would cause different symptoms.
questions.keyConcept: CPA tumors cause deafness and vertigo
options: Cerebello-pontine angle gives attachment to VI & VII cranial nerves.
Nervus intermedius is the medial root of the facial nerve.
VIII cranial nerve lies medial to VII cranial nerve.
Its ventral surface shows a sulcus for vertebral artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All the following structures wind around cerebral peduncles EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The optic nerve is an outpouching of the brain and does not wind around the cerebral peduncles; it runs in the optic tract to the lateral geniculate body. The trochlear nerve wraps around the cerebral peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Optic nerve does not wind around cerebral peduncle

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All the following form boundaries of interpeduncular fossa EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The optic nerve is not a boundary of the interpeduncular fossa. The boundaries are: cerebral peduncles (posterolateral), upper border of pons (inferior), optic chiasma (superior), and optic tract (posterolateral).
questions.keyConcept: Optic nerve not boundary of interpeduncular fossa

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Contents of interpeduncular fossa belong to:
questions.explanation: The interpeduncular fossa is located in the midbrain, between the cerebral peduncles. Its contents (oculomotor nerve, posterior perforated substance, etc.) are all midbrain structures.
questions.keyConcept: Interpeduncular fossa belongs to midbrain

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In dorsal surface of medulla oblongata, choose CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The vestibular trigone lies between the limbs of the inferior fovea in the floor of the fourth ventricle. This is the correct statement about dorsal medullary surface features.
questions.keyConcept: Vestibular trigone between limbs of inferior fovea
options: Gracile tubercle is the most medial structure of open medulla.
Base of open medulla is formed by medullary stria.
Vestibular trigone lies between limbs of inferior fovea.
Hypoglossal trigone forms most medial trigone of superior fovea.
Apex of open medulla is continuous with cerebral aqueduct.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards back of pons, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The medial eminence overlies the abducent nucleus, not the facial nucleus. The facial nucleus lies more laterally and is overlain by the facial colliculus formed by fibers wrapping around the abducent nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Medial eminence overlies abducent nucleus, not facial
options: Its apex is continuous with cerebral acqueduct.
Locus ceruleus lies at upper end of sulcus limitans.
Sulcus limitans lies lateral to medial eminence.
Vestibular area lies lateral to superior fovea.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: For each one of the boundaries of the 4th ventricle in the left column, choose the appropriate description in the right column:
questions.explanation: This matching tests knowledge of fourth ventricle boundaries: Superior medullary velum forms the superior roof; facial colliculus is in the pontine floor; inferior cerebellar peduncle forms lateral boundary; choroid plexus forms inferior roof; inferior fovea is in the medial floor.
questions.keyConcept: Superior medullary velum forms superior roof of 4th ventricle

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Posterior external arcuate fibers are axons of:
questions.explanation: Posterior external arcuate fibers originate from the accessory cuneate nucleus (lateral cuneate nucleus), which receives proprioceptive input from the upper limb. These fibers enter the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Accessory cuneate nucleus gives posterior arcuate fibers

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A collection of ascending fibers in the brain stem form:
questions.explanation: A lemniscus is a collection of sensory fibers that ascend through the brainstem. Examples include the medial lemniscus (fine touch/proprioception), spinal lemniscus (pain/temperature), and trigeminal lemniscus (face sensation).
questions.keyConcept: Lemniscus is collection of ascending fibers in brainstem

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The descending tracts run in the following part of the midbrain:
questions.explanation: The descending tracts (corticospinal, corticobulbar) run in the crus cerebri of the midbrain. The tegmentum contains ascending tracts and nuclei. The substantia nigra separates the crus from the tegmentum.
questions.keyConcept: Descending tracts in crus cerebri

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The internal arcuate fibers in the medulla are axons of:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are axons of second-order neurons in the dorsal column nuclei (gracile and cuneate nuclei). They decussate in the medulla to form the medial lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers from gracile/cuneate nuclei

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The fibers present in the medial 1/5 of the crus cerebri are:
questions.explanation: The frontal pontine fibers (from prefrontal cortex) occupy the medial one-fifth of the crus cerebri. Corticospinal fibers are in the middle three-fifths, and parieto/temporopontine fibers are in the lateral one-fifth.
questions.keyConcept: Frontopontine fibers in medial 1/5 of crus cerebri

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following olivary nuclear complex is not contained in medulla?
questions.explanation: The medial accessory olive is part of the olivary nuclear complex within the medulla. The superior olivary nucleus is in the pons, not the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Superior olivary nucleus not in medulla

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The fibers in the lateral 1/5 of crus cerebri include:
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus connects the vestibular nuclei with the nuclei of cranial nerves III, IV, and VI to coordinate eye movements. It also connects with the spinal cord for head and neck reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: MLF connects vestibular nuclei with III, IV, VI nuclei

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which one of the following is an afferent connection to the inferior colliculus:
questions.explanation: This matching tests midbrain structures: cerebral aqueduct (around which the tectal plate curves); trochlear nucleus (inferior to oculomotor); superior cerebellar peduncle (lateral to red nucleus).
questions.keyConcept: Superior cerebellar peduncle decussates in midbrain

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which one of the following decussations is associated with red nucleus?
questions.explanation: The nucleus ambiguus is the motor nucleus supplying muscles of the larynx (and pharynx/soft palate). It is the common motor nucleus for cranial nerves IX, X, and XI for these muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus supplies laryngeal muscles
options: Decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which one of the following ends in the VPMN of the thalamus?
questions.explanation: The nucleus solitarius (solitary nucleus) is the visceral afferent nucleus receiving general visceral afferent (GVA) and special visceral afferent (SVA - taste) fibers from CN VII, IX, and X.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus solitarius - visceral afferent column

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards the internal structure of the midbrain, choose the CORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: The nucleus ambiguus is the special visceral efferent (branchiomotor) nucleus for cranial nerves IX, X, and XI. It supplies stylopharyngeus (IX), pharynx/larynx muscles (X), and sternocleidomastoid/trapezius (XI).
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus - common motor for IX, X, XI
options: Parieto-pontine fibers - medial 1/5 of crus cerebri.
Ventral tegmental Decussation - tegmentum at level of inferior colliculus.
Cortico-spinal tract - lateral 1/5 of crus cerebri.
Cortico-nuclear tract - middle 3/5 of crus cerebri.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards the internal features of the medulla, choose for each structure in left column, its appropriate description in right column:
questions.explanation: The nucleus solitarius receives taste fibers (special visceral afferent) from the facial, glossopharyngeal, and vagus nerves. It is the only nucleus dedicated to visceral afferent processing.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus solitarius receives taste fibers

c. Decussation of internal arcuate fibers.
